promptHtml: You want to watch three nets of a design with an ILA as it runs on the board. Put the steps in order.
explanationHtml: The marks go in first, so that synthesis keeps the nets and their names. Set Up Debug works on the synthesised design: it makes the ILA from the marked nets and writes the commands into the constraints. Implementation then builds the ILA into the chip, and only a programmed board, with the probes file that names each probe, can be triggered.
steps: Put mark_debug on the nets you want to see, in the HDL.
Run Set Up Debug: choose the ILA's clock, its sample depth and its probes.
Implement the design and write the bitstream.
Program the board with the bitstream and the probes file, then run the trigger.

promptHtml: echo, the level's project, uses no block RAM. echo_ila is the same design with an ILA of 1024 samples on its 12 probe bits. Below is the Memory table of echo_ila's Utilization report.
explanationHtml: One RAMB18, half a block RAM tile, which is why the tile count reads 0.5. It holds the samples: 1024 samples of 12 bits are 12,288 bits, which fit in its 18 kilobits. A deeper ILA, or more probe bits, needs more of them.
excerpt: |     Site Type     | Used | Fixed | Prohibited | Available | Util% |
ask: How many RAMB18 blocks does echo_ila use?

promptHtml: You want an ILA to record one whole character on the board's rx line, from its start bit to its stop bit. At 115,200 baud a character lasts about 86.8 µs. With the trigger at the first sample of the window, which capture holds all of it?
explanationHtml: A capture lasts its sample depth times the clock period. 1024 samples of 10 ns are 10.24 µs and 4096 are 40.96 µs: both end long before the stop bit. A faster clock makes the window shorter, 5.12 µs at 200 MHz. 16384 samples last 163.84 µs, enough. Each sample costs block RAM, and the ILA stores one at every edge whatever its probes do. So it is often cheaper to watch uart_rx's data and valid and trigger on valid: the whole byte is on data in that one cycle, and 1024 samples show it.
options: 16384 samples at 100 MHz, triggered on rx falling.
1024 samples at 100 MHz, triggered on rx falling.
4096 samples at 100 MHz, triggered on rx falling.
1024 samples on a 200 MHz clock, triggered on rx falling.

promptHtml: echo, the level's project, uses 58 LUTs and 63 flip-flops. Below is the Slice Logic table of echo_ila, the same design with an ILA of 1024 samples on 12 probe bits.
explanationHtml: 1,174, twenty times echo's 58, and 1,960 flip-flops against 63. The ILA and the debug hub that links it to the JTAG port take over 1,100 LUTs to watch 12 bits: on a design that nearly fills the chip, that can be what no longer fits. An ILA is a tool for finding a bug, built in for as long as you need it.
excerpt: |          Site Type         | Used | Fixed | Prohibited | Available | Util% |
ask: How many LUTs does echo_ila use?

promptHtml: Below is the probe table of echo_ila's ILA, from its debug core report: each probe, its bits, and the net each bit watches. You want every capture to show the moment uart_rx hands a byte to the FIFO.
explanationHtml: Probe 1, which watches got_valid: uart_rx sets it to 1 for one cycle per byte, the cycle the byte on got is complete and goes into the FIFO. Triggering on it puts that cycle in every capture, with the byte on probe0 and the FIFO's count on probe2 around it. The bits of got change at every read while a byte comes in, so a trigger on one of them would also catch bytes half-received.
